title: When AI Takes Notes: Court Allows Privacy Claims Against Otter.ai to Proceed

reading.body:
A voice transcription service used during video meetings collected audio from private conversations to train its AI systems. The deployment relied on users clicking a checkbox to consent to data sharing, but the lawsuit alleges this consent was not sufficiently informed about how the audio would be used, creating a gap between what users thought they had agreed to and what the system actually did with their data.

The failure happened at the point where users encountered the permission mechanism. Catching it would have required either explicit disclosure of the data use practices before recording began, or obtaining separate informed consent from all meeting participants rather than relying on the meeting host's checkbox. The lawsuit also questions whether the company's process for removing identifying information from audio before using it to train models actually works, though not established is whether the de-identification was actually ineffective or whether any identifying information was actually recovered or misused.

Class-action suit claims Otter AI secretly records private work conversations
Otter.ai faces class action lawsuit for unauthorized meeting recording
Enterprise note-taking apps face legal scrutiny as Otter hit with privacy suit

summary:
A federal class-action lawsuit filed in California accuses Otter.ai, a Mountain View-based artificial intelligence company, of secretly recording private work conversations without permission. The suit claims that Otter's transcription service, which records virtual meetings on Zoom, Google Meet, and Microsoft Teams, collects audio data to train its AI systems without properly informing meeting participants. Plaintiff Justin Brewer alleges his privacy was violated when he discovered Otter had recorded a confidential conversation. The lawsuit contends the company violates state and federal privacy and wiretap laws and profits from this covert recording practice.

Otter.ai serves approximately 25 million users who have participated in over 1 billion recorded meetings since the company's founding in 2016. While Otter's privacy policy states users grant permission through a checkbox, the lawsuit maintains many users are deceived about data sharing. Previous incidents have raised concerns, including cases where sensitive business information was shared and where data sharing raised fears about foreign government access. The lawsuit questions whether Otter's method of anonymizing audio data before feeding it into machine learning systems is effective, noting the company provides no public explanation of its de-identification process.
